title: Stop waiting on 15-minute file drops: subscribe to RailClear bus
subtitle: Recommendation to Priya Nair and Marcus Bell on ingest path for recon legs. Kafka over FTP, over S3+SQS, and over polling the same drop every 60 seconds.
author: Aman Kumar
audience: Priya Nair (EM), Marcus Bell (Clearhaven TAM), Helen Cho (ops), Diego Alvarez (SRE), Kavya Menon, Rahul Deshmukh
owners: Aman Kumar (author), Kavya Menon (consumer work), Diego Alvarez (MSK and IAM)
related: CLH-TDD-2022-021, CLH-1887 (FTP lockouts), CLH-2031 (truncated drop 2023-01-19), CLH-2104 (match lag), NS-RECON-441, CLH-TDD-2023-008 (follow-on Kafka redesign)
summary: We should subscribe to the RailClear bus they already emit, and retire the 15-minute FTP file drop as the primary ingest path for recon.fact_leg. Mean time from RailClear emit to first match cycle is 40.2 minutes today. Helen Cho's target is under 10. The 60-second poller idea does not get us there and it makes the FTP user she already wants gone even noisier. S3+SQS is cheaper on paper and still batch-shaped. This memo is the decision record for Priya and Marcus, with cost, ops load, bad-file behavior, and a concrete cutover so Kavya and Diego can price the work.
form_description: Internal recommendation memo from Aman Kumar to Priya Nair and Marcus Bell comparing three ingest options for Clearhaven recon and taking a position for Kafka on the existing RailClear bus.
revision_history: Draft numbers from CLH-2104 lag extract and Helen's FTP notes.
Added S3+SQS cost from Chris Patel. Rejected 60s poller after Helen's comment in #clh-recon.
Corrected bus topic name (rc.settlement.leg.v1, not rc.legs). Added DLQ sketch.
Priya asked for a one-page decision block at the top. This version.

blocks.text: Who this is for and what I want you to decide

Priya, Marcus: I need a go/no-go on ingest. We have been treating the RailClear 15-minute file drop as the source of truth since the recon platform stood up in September. That choice is why Helen's match window keeps slipping past 7:20pm ET on busy days, and it is why Diego still has an FTP user on the allowlist that compliance reviews every quarter. RailClear told Marcus in December that the same payload already lands on a queue they call bus. We never subscribed. I want us to subscribe, run dual-ingest for three settlement weeks, then turn the drop into a fallback only.

This is not a platform rewrite. ingest-api, match-engine, and break-svc stay. The change is how a leg record gets into recon.ingest_staging before the matcher runs. Kavya estimated 9.5 engineering days for the consumer plus DLQ. Diego estimated 4 days for MSK topics, IAM, and the Grafana lag board. I put $26.2k annual run cost against the current $2.4k FTP bill plus the 0.6 FTE we already burn on drop failures. The dollar line is not the argument. Time-to-match and bad-file blast radius are.

blocks.label: Recommendation
blocks.text: Adopt Kafka on RailClear bus topic rc.settlement.leg.v1 as the primary ingest path. Keep the 15-minute file drop as a cold fallback for 90 days, then disable the poller. Do not poll FTP every 60 seconds. Do not build an S3+SQS sidecar as the primary path. Target: p50 emit-to-match under 8.4 minutes, p95 under 12 minutes, by the April 11 cutover window (CLH-TDD-2023-008 will pick up the consumer internals).
Decision for a VP skim

Keep doing what we do and we will keep missing Helen's 7:20pm close on month-end, because the file itself often does not land until 16 to 22 minutes after RailClear has already computed the legs. Switching to bus cuts that wait. S3+SQS looks tidy and still waits on RailClear's batch writer, which they said they would not change this year. Polling FTP faster does not change when the file is written, and it multiplies the credential we are trying to kill.

blocks.caption: Option scorecard for Priya / Marcus. Costs are 12-month run plus implementation labor at loaded $148/hr.
rows: One object; matcher can have a hole

blocks.text: Lab numbers for Kafka are from Kavya's soak on msk-clh-dev.nseng.internal last week, 1.14M synthetic legs replayed from the January 19 dump, match-engine at current prod replica count (6). We did not have RailClear's real bus in that soak. Marcus has a written note from their TAM, Lena Ortiz, that rc.settlement.leg.v1 schema matches the drop columns we already parse, plus a bus_offset and bus_published_at we do not have today. If that note is wrong we find out in week one of dual-ingest, not after we delete FTP.
Current path, with the ugly numbers

RailClear writes a gzipped CSV to ftp-drop-01.clearhaven.internal every 15 minutes during the settlement window, roughly 14:05 to 19:35 ET on business days. Filename pattern is RC_LEGS_YYYYMMDD_HHMM.csv.gz. The poller recon-file-poller runs as a CronJob in namespace recon on eks-clh-prod-use1, schedule */15 * * * *, catching the clock on :00/:15/:30/:45. If the file is 90 seconds late, which happened 17 times in January, we wait a full extra cycle. Helen's runbook then says wait for the next drop rather than SSH, because the last time someone pulled a partial file we loaded 14,200 legs with empty account_no (CLH-2031, January 19).

Mean time-to-match in January, measured as RailClear's file mtime minus match-engine's first commit of that batch_id into recon.match_result, was 40.2 minutes. p50 was 37.4. p95 was 61.8. Month-end January 31 was 67.3 minutes p95 because the 18:15 drop was 214 MB uncompressed and ingest-api sat on a single pod during a rollout Priya had already frozen. Chris Patel pulled this from the Datadog span ingest.parse to match.commit, joined to the FTP mtime Diego scrapes into recon.drop_manifest. I trust the join. The 40 minute number is not a vibe.

blocks.caption: January 2023 drop performance. Source: recon.drop_manifest + Datadog APM, Chris Patel extract 2023-02-01.

blocks.text: The FTP user is svc_railclear_ftp. Password rotates every 90 days through a ticket Helen files with their IAM, then Diego pastes into the k8s secret recon/ftp-drop. That secret has been wrong twice since October. Each time the poller looked healthy because the CronJob succeeded with 'no new files' and match-engine processed an empty batch. Helen noticed because the break count on her dashboard went to 11, which is the 'we got nothing' tell, not because we had an alert on drop_manifest.row_count = 0. Diego added that alert on January 20. It has already fired twice on genuine empty files at 14:15 when RailClear had a holiday calendar mismatch. So the alert is noisy and we still do not know if a drop is late versus empty versus truncated until someone opens the file.
What a bad file actually does today

CLH-2031 is the one I keep citing because we have the timeline. 16:15 ET drop on January 19 was 11.4 MB gzip, advertised 186,441 rows in the RailClear trailer. The TCP session reset at 94% according to vsftpd log on ftp-drop-01. Poller saw a .gz, gunzip succeeded (gzip does not always fail on truncation the way people think), CSV parser accepted 172,188 rows, 14,253 of them with null account_no because the last field of a split line landed in the wrong column. ingest-api wrote them. match-engine created 9,418 breaks against positions that were fine. Helen spent 2.4 hours with me and Kavya deleting by batch_id 20230119-1615 and waiting for the 16:30 drop, which itself was late. Total match delay that afternoon: 73 minutes past her 7:20 target. The replay was SSH to ingest-worker-04 and a Python one-liner Kavya still has in her notes. There is no ops button. That is a different PRD.

If we keep FTP, the blast radius of a bad file is the whole drop. Always. The poller has no row-level checksum. RailClear's trailer count is a hint, not a constraint we enforce, because on December 8 the trailer was wrong and the file was fine, and we blocked a good batch (CLH-1762). After that fight we stopped enforcing the trailer. So we have neither a hard count check nor a partial-file detector. Diego can add a Content-Length compare against the FTP SIZE command. That catches some truncations. It does not catch a well-formed file with swapped columns, which is what happened on November 3 when RailClear added executing_broker as column 17 and we were still on 16.
Option A: keep the 15-minute drop

Doing nothing is a decision. The matcher is fine. The schema is fine. The delay is upstream of us. Marcus can keep asking RailClear to write files faster. Lena Ortiz already said no for 2023. Their file writer is a shared job across four introducing brokers and they will not special-case Clearhaven. If we stay here, I want Priya to tell Helen the 7:20pm target is not a control we own on month-end, and I want Diego to budget the FTP lockouts as a standing item. I do not think that conversation will go well, which is why I wrote the rest of this memo.

Cost to keep: $2.4k/year for the FTP VM (ftp-drop-01 is an m5.large in Clearhaven's account, we rebill). Ops load is the 0.6 FTE I mentioned, split roughly 0.35 Helen (waiting, reconciling, filing tickets) and 0.25 Diego plus me (secrets, poller, the January 19 cleanup). There is no engineering project. Time-to-match stays in the 37-67 minute band. Bad file: whole batch, manual delete, wait for next drop or SSH replay.
Option B: poll every 60 seconds (rejected)

Helen floated this in Slack on January 24 after the third late drop of the week. Rahul asked me to cost it. I did. Then I sat with Helen for twenty minutes and she said the sentence I am going to quote because I do not want us to relitigate this in April.
I already hate that FTP user. If you make it talk to us 15 times more often I will file the ticket to kill it myself. Get the data another way.

The engineering case is also weak. RailClear writes on a 15-minute wall clock. Polling at 60 seconds shaves the wait after the file appears, which is usually 0-14 minutes of sitting on the CronJob boundary. Chris modeled January with a simulated 60s poller against actual mtimes. p50 emit-to-match went from 40.2 to 28.7 minutes. p95 from 61.8 to 54.1. We do not get under 10. The remaining 20-plus minutes is parse + match + the fact that the file was not written yet. We would also open 15 times as many FTP control connections from the cluster. vsftpd on ftp-drop-01 already rate-limits auth failures. CLH-1887 was three lockouts in Q4 when a bad secret retried. A 60s poller with a stale secret would lock the user in under four minutes. Diego's words: 'please do not.'

blocks.label: Rejected: 60-second poller
blocks.text: Does not hit the under-10-minute target. Increases FTP auth surface that Helen and compliance already want gone. Best-case January replay still at 28.7 min p50. Do not pick this as a 'quick win' while Kafka is in flight. If someone proposes it again, point at CLH-1887 and this memo.
Option C: S3 + SQS

Chris Patel likes this because we already have clh-railclear-drops-prod in the Clearhaven AWS account for the nightly position snapshot. The pitch: RailClear writes the same gzip to s3://clh-railclear-drops-prod/legs/YYYY/MM/DD/HHMM.csv.gz, bucket notification to SQS queue clh-drop-notify-prod, ingest-api long-polls SQS, downloads the object, parses, done. No FTP user. Object versioning. Checksum in s3 etag or a sidecar .sha256, our choice.

Two problems. First, RailClear's file writer is still the clock. Lena said they can land a copy in S3 'in the same job' that writes FTP, which means the object appears when the file appears, not when the leg is computed. We measured their job: compute finishes, then a 3.4 to 9.1 minute pack-and-write. S3 does not remove that. Chris's model with instant SQS delivery still sits at 22.4 min p50 emit-to-match, because emit for us means 'RailClear knew the leg,' not 'object landed.' Second, a bad object is cleaner than a bad FTP file (we can checksum before parse) and worse for holes. If object N fails checksum and object N+1 succeeds, match-engine will process N+1 against a settlement_date that is missing a slice of N. Breaks look like genuine unmatched shorts. We saw a cousin of this in November when two drops arrived out of order after a poller retry. Helen had to explain to her desk why 4,100 breaks appeared and vanished. SQS FIFO with group-id = settlement_date would preserve order. It would also stall the day on a poison object until someone deleted it. That is an ops action we still do not have a UI for.

Year-1 cash is genuinely low: $186/month blended for PUT/GET plus SQS, say $2.2k, plus one more S3 replication to the Northstar bucket we use for forensics, $4.1k total. Implementation is 11 engineering days (ingest-api SQS consumer, IAM, a poison-object path, Datadog on ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible). I would take this as a fallback lander in 2024 if RailClear ever kills bus. I would not take it as the 2023 primary path because it does not hit the latency target and it keeps us coupled to their batch writer.

blocks.text: Option D: Kafka on the bus they already have

RailClear runs a Kafka-compatible bus at bus.railclear.net:9093, TLS, SASL/SCRAM. Topic rc.settlement.leg.v1, 24 partitions, retention 3 days according to Lena's email dated December 14. Message is JSON, one leg per record, keys we already know (account_no, cusip, settle_date, qty, side, executing_broker, contra, net_amt, source_ref) plus bus_offset, bus_published_at, and schema_id. They have been producing this since at least August. We never created a consumer group. I asked Marcus why. He said nobody on our side requested credentials and their default posture is 'file drop unless you ask.' We did not ask.

The work on our side is a new consumer in ingest-api (or a small sibling service, Kavya prefers sibling so a poison consumer crash does not take the HTTP API with it). I agree. Call it ingest-bus-consumer, Helm chart next to ingest-api, same namespace, same IRSA role plus a k8s secret for the SCRAM user. Consumer group clh.recon.leg.v1. We write recon.ingest_staging exactly as the poller does, with ingest_source = 'bus' and bus_offset stored so we can prove a row. match-engine does not change. Idempotency is the existing unique key on (account_no, cusip, settle_date, source_ref). Dual-ingest for three weeks means a row may arrive twice. The unique key is why that is acceptable. If the unique key is wrong we will find out on day one of dual-ingest, which is the point of dual-ingest.
Time-to-match math

Bus publish happens when RailClear's matcher commits, which Lena said is 40-90 seconds after their internal compute, not after the file pack. File pack is the slow part. If we consume with lag under 5 seconds, which is what we saw on msk-clh-dev with 1.14M messages and 6 match-engine pods, the remaining time is parse-to-staging (1.2-3.8 s per 10k messages in Kavya's bench) plus match-engine's current cycle (4.1-7.6 min on a normal day, 9.4 min on January 31). Add those and you get why I wrote 6.8 min p50 / 11.4 min p95 in the scorecard. Month-end will still be the ugly one because match-engine, not ingest, is the bound. That is a capacity memo, not this memo. Getting ingest out of the way is the part we can do in this quarter.
Cost

We do not consume RailClear's cluster from prod workloads directly if Diego can help it. His plan: MirrorMaker 2 from bus.railclear.net into our MSK cluster msk-clh-prod.nseng.internal (three kafka.m5.large, already running for the break-svc audit topic that almost nobody uses). Mirror the one topic. Our consumers stay inside the VPC. MSK is already $1,840/month for those three brokers. Incremental cost of one more topic with 1.4M messages/day at ~1.1 KB is small, Diego's back-of-envelope $340/month in cross-AZ and the RailClear egress they will rebill, which Marcus thinks is $0 because they wanted someone to use bus. I am still putting $340 in the model until we have a written waiver. Year-1 run $26.2k is the existing MSK allocation plus a 15% overhead Diego wants for a fourth broker if we start mirroring positions later. Implementation labor: 9.5 days Kavya+me, 4 days Diego, loaded $148/hr = $15.9k. I would rather spend that than another year of Helen's afternoons.

blocks.caption: Cost build-up. Diego's MSK invoice is AWS-CLH-MSK-2023-01. Labor is Northstar loaded rate.
rows: Already paid. Break-svc audit topic is 11 msg/min.
Drop if Marcus gets the waiver.
FTP we can stop after 90 days

blocks.text: Ops load

Pages we have today are FTP lockout, empty drop, truncated drop, poller CronJob failed, and Helen's 'why is match not done.' After cutover the FTP pages go away. New pages: consumer lag > 30k messages for 3 minutes, DLQ depth > 0, MM2 mirror lag > 15 seconds, SCRAM auth failures. Diego will own the first three alerts. Kavya will own DLQ replay runbook, which is offset-reset plus a documented kubectl job, not SSH onto a random worker. I expect 1.7 pages/month once it is boring, based on how break-svc's unused audit topic behaves (almost never) plus a guess at RailClear producer quality. If their schema_id changes without a last-byte compatible add, we will page. That is a feature.
Bad message, not bad file

A poison JSON record goes to topic rc.settlement.leg.v1.dlq after 3 failures in the consumer (retry, then skip). The rest of the partition continues. match-engine never sees the poison row. Helen sees a DLQ count on the same Grafana board, not 9,418 mystery breaks. The missing leg may still be a real break against the position file, so she is not blind. She is not drowning in false breaks from a truncated CSV either. Replay of the DLQ is a documented job that dumps the record, a human decides, and we produce it onto a retry topic. We are not editing payloads in a UI. Compliance already said no to that for a different ticket. Same answer here.

Schema drift is the remaining ugly case. If RailClear adds a field, we ignore it. If they rename account_no, we DLQ everything until Kavya ships a parser bump. Dual-ingest against the file drop is how we notice: drop row counts vs bus row counts per 15-minute window, alert if they diverge by more than 0.4% for two consecutive windows. Chris will build that comparison in recon.ingest_source_reconcile. If the file dies in 90 days, that comparison dies with it, and we live on DLQ plus a daily total vs RailClear's email of 'we published N legs.' I want that email as a contract item Marcus owns.
What I need from RailClear (Marcus)

items: SCRAM user clh-recon-ro on bus.railclear.net, ACL read on rc.settlement.leg.v1 and describe on the cluster. Rotate every 90 days to the same Secrets Manager path Diego already uses.
Written confirmation that bus_published_at is set at compute commit, not at file-write time. If it is file-write time, the latency case collapses and we should stop.
Retention 3 days is tight for a Friday night fail. Ask for 7 days. If they say no, we mirror with 7-day retention on our MSK copy and that becomes the source we rewind.
A daily published_count they already have internally, emailed or dropped to the same S3 bucket Chris uses, so we can reconcile after FTP is gone.
A named on-call on their side for schema_id changes. Lena is TAM, not on-call. We got burned on November 3 with a silent column add.

blocks.text: Cutover plan an engineer can run

We do not flip a flag on a Thursday at 16:10. Dual-ingest, then fallback, then disable. Priya signs the change ticket. Helen is in the Zoom for the first two settlement days. Diego has MM2 lag on his screen. I am on the consumer. Kavya has the parser.

items: Week of Feb 13: Diego creates MSK topic railclear.leg.v1 (24 partitions, rf=3, retention 168h) and MM2 connector railclear-bus-mm2 in msk-clh-prod. Confirm lag with kafka-consumer-groups. Do not point ingest at it yet.

Week of Feb 13: Kavya ships ingest-bus-consumer to clh-nonprod. Replay 2.2 hours of mirrored traffic. Compare row counts to the FTP drop for the same window. Gate: divergence under 0.4% and zero uncaught parse exceptions.

Week of Feb 20: dual-ingest in prod, ingest_source='bus' writes alongside the poller. Unique key swallows dupes. recon.ingest_source_reconcile job runs every 15 minutes. Helen ignores bus-origin rows on her break board (we will tag them) until Priya says otherwise.
Three full settlement weeks with divergence under 0.4% and DLQ under 20 messages/day. If we miss, we do not cut. January 31-shaped days are the ones that count. Do not certify on a quiet Tuesday.

Cutover change ticket NS-CHG-2023-094, target Tuesday April 11 10:05 ET, outside Helen's freeze. Poller CronJob suspend. Consumer replicas 3. Watch lag and match p50 for the 14:05-19:35 window. Rollback is unsuspend the CronJob (one kubectl). FTP files will have piled up; poller catches them.
FTP remains landing for 90 days as cold fallback. After July 10, Diego disables svc_railclear_ftp and we tell RailClear to stop the drop. Marcus owns that email.

blocks.caption: Commands Diego and I will run on cutover day. Cluster msk-clh-prod.nseng.internal, namespace recon.
blocks.text:
# confirm mirror lag (should be < 5s under normal produce)
kubectl -n recon exec deploy/mm2-railclear -- \
  kafka-consumer-groups.sh --bootstrap-server msk-clh-prod.nseng.internal:9092 \
  --group connect-railclear-bus-mm2 --describe

# consumer group lag after cutover
kubectl -n recon exec deploy/ingest-bus-consumer -- \
  kafka-consumer-groups.sh --bootstrap-server msk-clh-prod.nseng.internal:9092 \
  --group clh.recon.leg.v1 --describe

# suspend FTP poller (rollback = set spec.suspend=false)
kubectl -n recon patch cronjob recon-file-poller -p '{"spec":{"suspend":true}}'

# DLQ depth
kubectl -n recon exec deploy/ingest-bus-consumer -- \
  kafka-run-class.sh kafka.tools.GetOffsetShell \
  --broker-list msk-clh-prod.nseng.internal:9092 \
  --topic rc.settlement.leg.v1.dlq --time -1

# if we have to unsuspend in a hurry
kubectl -n recon patch cronjob recon-file-poller -p '{"spec":{"suspend":false}}'
kubectl -n recon create job recon-file-poller-now --from=cronjob/recon-file-poller
Failure modes I actually worry about

MM2 silently stops mirroring. Consumer lag looks fine because it is caught up on a stale MSK topic. match-engine looks fine because it is matching yesterday. Helen's break count is the tell again. Mitigation: alert on bus.railclear.net end-offset vs MSK end-offset, sampled every 30 seconds, page at 15 seconds of divergence. Diego owns the probe. If that probe is not in place we do not cut.

Unique key is wrong and dual-ingest double-writes. We would see recon.fact_leg grow at 2x and match-engine CPU follow. Mitigation: the reconcile job also compares fact_leg counts per settle_date against RailClear published_count. Alert at 1.6x. If it fires on day one of dual-ingest we stop the consumer and stay on FTP. That is an acceptable embarrassment.

SCRAM password rotates on their side and nobody tells us. Consumer auth-fails, lag climbs, we page, Helen is mid-window. Mitigation: 7-day overlap on old and new password, Diego's runbook, a calendar invite 10 days before the 90-day mark. Same operational shape as the FTP secret, minus the lockout amplifier.

RailClear publishes a burst at 19:05 that is 8.2M legs (their month-end shape, even if our daily is 1.4M). Consumer survives. match-engine is the one that falls over, which it already does on FTP month-end. Kafka does not make that worse. It makes it start 20 minutes earlier, which Helen actually wants. Capacity for match-engine is Rahul's FY23 Q2 thread, not a reason to keep FTP.
Open questions and owners

blocks.caption: Open items as of February 7. Priya asked for names, not 'the team.'

Yes. If file-write, Kafka case weakens.
7-day retention on their topic, or we keep 7 days on MSK only?

No. I prefer sibling. Priya can overrule.
Who pays the $340 egress if they rebill?

No. Button is a later PRD.
Rina Das: any PG write-pattern change from smaller, earlier batches?
No for cutover. Yes for her vacuum schedule.

blocks.text: Rina is on this list because I mentioned the plan in passing and she asked whether fact_leg inserts would arrive as a 15-minute lump or as a trickle. Trickle. That is friendlier for autovacuum on recon.fact_leg, which already hurts her at 18:40 on month-end. She does not need to sign this memo. She does need a heads-up before April 11 so she is not surprised by a different write shape. I will send her the soak graphs from msk-clh-dev.
What I am not asking for

I am not asking to rewrite match-engine. I am not asking for a schema registry project, though Kavya will drop a jsonschema file in the consumer repo and fail closed on required field loss. I am not asking Helen to learn offset math. I am not asking to kill the drop on day one. I am not asking for S3+SQS 'while we wait for Kafka,' because that is two ingest projects and one target, and the 60-second poller already tried to be the cheap version of that impulse.

Rahul asked whether this should be a PRD. It can become one if Priya wants a numbered requirements list. The requirements are: subscribe to the existing bus, beat 10 minutes p50 on emit-to-match, do not enlarge the FTP user, survive a poison message without a 9k-break afternoon, and give Diego a rollback that is one kubectl. That is the whole product.
Ask

Priya: approve Kafka on RailClear bus as primary ingest, dual-ingest start week of February 20, cutover target April 11, FTP fallback 90 days. Reject the 60-second poller in writing so it does not come back as a March 'interim.' Marcus: get the SCRAM user and the bus_published_at answer this week. Helen: I need you in the dual-ingest reviews, not as a signer, as the person who will tell us the break board looks wrong. Diego: MM2 this sprint. Kavya: consumer skeleton is already in her fork; I will review Thursday.

blocks.label: If we do nothing
blocks.text: January numbers repeat. Helen keeps a 7:20 target we miss on month-end. The FTP user stays on the compliance list. The next truncated gzip costs another 2.4 hours and another round of SSH. RailClear already built the queue. We are the ones not using it.
